stories.text: In about 1829 cottages were built for Ruddington's framework knitters, who worked at hand frames in workshops behind them; the workshops date from about 1840. All are listed, and together they now make up the Framework Knitters' Museum.

stories.text: John Leavers lived here, at Canning Circus, where a plaque calls him the inventor of the Leavers lace machine, in 1813. He improved John Heathcoat's lace machine, and in 1821 emigrated to Grand-Couronne in Normandy.

Garners Hill, said to be the oldest site in Nottingham, once held cave dwellings, a Saxon fort and a medieval town hall, until the Victorians cleared it for a railway line. On 14 November 2009 an art centre designed by Caruso St John opened here, its walls embossed with a Nottingham lace pattern.

74224.sum: Nottingham Contemporary (formerly known as the Centre for Contemporary Art Nottingham) is a contemporary art centre in the Lace Market area of Nottingham, England. The gallery opened in 2009. The gallery describes its site as being "the oldest in the city", having been the site of a Saxon fort.

stories.text: The congregation went back to 1690 and became Unitarian in 1802. In 1876 it built this chapel, to designs by Stuart Colman. Worship ended in 1982; the chapel then housed a lace museum, and it is now a Pitcher & Piano.

74438.sum: High Pavement Chapel is a redundant church building in Nottingham, Nottinghamshire, England. It is now the Pitcher & Piano public house and is Grade II listed. It was built as, and for most of its existence operated as, a Unitarian place of worship.

stories.text: Built from 1854 to designs by Thomas Chambers Hine for Thomas Adams, a Quaker lace manufacturer, and opened in 1855 as his lace showroom and warehouse, with a chapel for the workers in the basement. Inspectors thought it a model example of its kind; since 1999 it has been part of Nottingham College.
The lace manufacturer Thomas Adams built this showroom and warehouse; it is named after him.[^s1][^s2]
The Nottingham architect Thomas Chambers Hine designed this lace showroom and warehouse.[^s1][^s2]

74534.sum: The Adams Building, formerly the Adams and Page warehouse on Stoney Street, is the largest building in the Lace Market district of the city of Nottingham in England. Now Grade II*-listed by Historic England, the Adams Building was formerly a lace showroom and warehouse. Since 1999, it has formed part of the city campus of what is now Nottingham College.

stories.text: In 1778 George, James and John Robinson took a 56-year lease from Frederick Montagu to build cotton mills on the Leen. With Castle Mill, Grange Farm, Middle Mill and Forge Mill, and the dam and Moor Pond that fed them, they employed around 800 people, many of them apprentices brought from the St Marylebone workhouse in London. In 1785 James Robinson bought a Boulton and Watt engine for the mill at Bestwood, said to be the first rotative steam engine in a cotton mill anywhere. Spinning had stopped by 1828, and most of the buildings were taken down in the 1850s.

178285.sum: Forge Mill is a commercial building on Mill Lane. The building was built in 1787, according to Historic England (via Wikipedia). It is Grade II listed.

stories.text: The mill owner John Hawksley built a large cotton mill here, working before the end of 1791 with a 60-horsepower engine, and laid out Arnot Hill Park in about 1792 as a setting for his house. His son Thomas Hawksley, born at Arnot Hill House in 1807, became the engineer who gave Nottingham clean water. The house is listed Grade II.

The water engineer Thomas Hawksley was born at Arnot Hill House in 1807. His Trent Bridge waterworks, completed in 1831, gave Britain its first high-pressure constant supply, which kept dirty water out of the mains.
